choices.text: It is a different vector, because it starts somewhere new
It is the same vector: same magnitude and same direction
It is the same vector only if it starts at the origin
It is a position vector for the new start point

questions.explanation: The trap claim is: Moving a vector to a new start point changes it. A free vector is fixed by its magnitude and direction alone: the redrawn arrow still moves 2 right and 3 up, so it is the same vector. Only a position vector is pinned to the origin.
questions.misconception: Moving a vector to a new start point changes it.
questions.prompt: The arrow for a vector moves 2 right and 3 up. The same arrow is redrawn starting at a different point, still moving 2 right and 3 up. What can we say about the redrawn arrow?

questions.explanation: Magnitude is Pythagoras on the components: sqrt(2^2 + 3^2) = sqrt(4 + 9) = sqrt(13). The choice 5 adds the components, and 13 forgets the square root.
questions.prompt: What is the magnitude of the vector (2, 3)?

questions.explanation: Adding vectors tail to head adds the components one pair at a time: the right moves add, and the up moves add. The sum runs from the very first tail to the very last head.
questions.prompt: Add a = (2, 3) and b = (1, -1), and state the column vector a + b.

questions.explanation: The dot product multiplies matching components and adds: 2 x 4 from the right moves and 3 x (-1) from the up moves. It is a scalar, not a vector.
questions.prompt: Find the dot product a . b for a = (2, 3) and b = (4, -1).

questions.explanation: Perpendicular means dot product zero: (1, 1, -1) . (1, 2, 3) = 1 + 2 - 3 = 0. The others give 1, 2 and 6, so none of them is perpendicular to n.
questions.prompt: Which vector is perpendicular to the normal n = (1, 2, 3)?
